# Unit 1: Introduction to biochemistry and carbohydrates

This unit covers syllabus chapters 1 (introduction, 2 hours) and 2 (carbohydrates, 5 hours).

## 1.1 What is biochemistry?

**Biochemistry** is the study of the chemical substances present in living things and of the chemical reactions that take place in living cells. It explains life in the language of chemistry: what the body is made of (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins, minerals, water) and how these substances are built up, broken down and controlled.

The word comes from "bios" (life) and "chemistry". The chemical reactions of the body taken together are called **metabolism**.

## 1.2 Scope of biochemistry in pharmacy

A pharmacist needs biochemistry in almost every area of work.

| Area | How biochemistry helps |
| --- | --- |
| How drugs act | Many drugs act on enzymes or receptors (statins block HMG-CoA reductase, allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, aspirin blocks cyclooxygenase). |
| Drug metabolism | Liver enzymes (cytochrome P450 in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum) change drugs into other forms; this decides dose and drug interactions. |
| Diagnosis | Blood and urine tests (glucose, urea, creatinine, cholesterol, bilirubin, enzymes such as SGPT) are biochemical tests. Pharmacists in hospitals and laboratories read these reports. |
| Nutrition and supplements | Knowledge of vitamins, minerals, amino acids and oral rehydration salts helps in counselling and in choosing supplements. |
| Biotechnology products | Insulin, vaccines, interferons and monoclonal antibodies are made by recombinant DNA technology. |
| Disease understanding | Diabetes mellitus, jaundice, phenylketonuria, gout and fatty liver are disorders of metabolism. |
| Formulation | Enzymes and proteins in formulations (pancreatin, papain) need suitable pH and temperature for stability. |
| Clinical pathology laboratory | A D.Pharm holder may help in a clinical laboratory; the practical part of this subject trains for it. |

## 1.3 The cell and its biochemical organization

The **cell** is the structural and functional unit of life. Cells are of two types.

| Feature | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Example | Bacteria | Human, animal, plant and fungal cells |
| Nucleus | No true nucleus; DNA lies free in the cytoplasm (nucleoid) | True nucleus with a nuclear membrane |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes) |
| Ribosomes | 70S | 80S in cytoplasm (70S in mitochondria) |
| Size | Small, about 1–10 µm | Larger, about 10–100 µm |

### Organelles and their biochemical functions

```text
                 ┌──────────────── Plasma membrane ────────────────┐
                 │   Cytosol: glycolysis, HMP shunt,                │
                 │   fatty acid synthesis, glycogen metabolism      │
                 │                                                  │
                 │   ┌──────────┐    Rough ER ═══ (ribosomes)       │
                 │   │ Nucleus  │    Smooth ER ── drug metabolism   │
                 │   │  DNA,    │                                   │
                 │   │ nucleolus│    Golgi  ))) packing, glycosylation
                 │   └──────────┘                                   │
                 │   (Mitochondrion) TCA, β-oxidation, ETC, ATP     │
                 │   (Lysosome) hydrolytic enzymes                  │
                 │   (Peroxisome) catalase, H2O2 breakdown          │
                 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Part of the cell | Biochemical function |
| --- | --- |
| **Plasma membrane** | Lipid bilayer of phospholipids with cholesterol and proteins (fluid mosaic model, Singer and Nicolson, 1972). Selective permeability, transport of nutrients and drugs, receptors for hormones. |
| **Nucleus** | Holds DNA (genetic material). DNA replication and transcription (RNA synthesis) take place here. The **nucleolus** makes ribosomal RNA. |
| **Mitochondria** ("power house") | Tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, β-oxidation of fatty acids, electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation (ATP formation), ketone body formation, part of the urea cycle. Have their own DNA. |
| **Rough endoplasmic reticulum** | Ribosomes on its surface make proteins, especially proteins for export (secretory proteins). |
| **Smooth endoplasmic reticulum** | Synthesis of lipids and steroids; metabolism of drugs and toxins by cytochrome P450 enzymes (the "microsomal" enzymes). |
| **Golgi apparatus** | Modifies proteins (adds sugar chains – glycosylation), packs them into vesicles and sends them to their destination. |
| **Lysosomes** ("suicide bags") | Contain acid hydrolases (proteases, lipases, nucleases) that digest worn-out parts and engulfed bacteria. |
| **Peroxisomes** | Contain catalase and oxidases; destroy hydrogen peroxide; oxidise very long chain fatty acids. |
| **Ribosomes** | Site of protein synthesis (translation of mRNA). |
| **Cytosol** | Glycolysis, hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt, fatty acid synthesis, glycogen synthesis and breakdown. |

## 1.4 Carbohydrates: definition

**Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or compounds that give these on hydrolysis.

Many have the general formula **Cn(H2O)n**, which is why they were once called "hydrates of carbon". The formula is not a strict rule: deoxyribose (C5H10O4) does not fit it, while lactic acid (C3H6O3) fits it but is not a carbohydrate.

## 1.5 Classification of carbohydrates

```text
                       Carbohydrates
        ┌──────────────┬──────┴────────┬──────────────────┐
 Monosaccharides  Disaccharides  Oligosaccharides   Polysaccharides
 (one sugar unit) (two units)    (3–10 units)       (more than 10 units)
                                                    ┌──────┴──────┐
                                              Homopolysaccharides  Heteropolysaccharides
```

### Monosaccharides

They cannot be hydrolysed into simpler sugars. They are classified by the **number of carbon atoms** and by the **functional group** (aldehyde = aldose; ketone = ketose).

| Carbon atoms | Name | Aldose example | Ketose example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | Triose | Glyceraldehyde | Dihydroxyacetone |
| 4 | Tetrose | Erythrose | Erythrulose |
| 5 | Pentose | Ribose, xylose, arabinose | Ribulose, xylulose |
| 6 | Hexose | Glucose, galactose, mannose | Fructose |
| 7 | Heptose | Glucoheptose | Sedoheptulose |

### Disaccharides

Two monosaccharides joined by a **glycosidic bond**: maltose, lactose, sucrose (details in 1.8).

### Oligosaccharides

3 to 10 monosaccharide units, for example raffinose (a trisaccharide) and the sugar chains of glycoproteins.

### Polysaccharides (glycans)

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Homopolysaccharides | Made of one kind of monosaccharide | Starch, glycogen, cellulose, dextrin (all glucose); inulin (fructose) |
| Heteropolysaccharides | Made of two or more kinds of units | Heparin, hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulphate (mucopolysaccharides), agar, gums |

## 1.6 Chemical properties of carbohydrates

1. **Reducing property.** Sugars with a free (or potentially free) aldehyde or ketone group reduce mild oxidising agents such as alkaline copper sulphate (Benedict's and Fehling's reagents). Cupric ions (blue) are reduced to cuprous oxide (red). All monosaccharides, maltose and lactose are reducing; sucrose is non-reducing.
2. **Osazone formation.** Reducing sugars heated with phenylhydrazine give yellow crystals called osazones. Their shape helps identify the sugar. Glucose, fructose and mannose give the same osazone because the reaction involves carbons 1 and 2 only.
3. **Mutarotation.** A freshly made solution of glucose slowly changes its optical rotation until it reaches a fixed value. This happens because the α and β forms of glucose change into each other through the open-chain form until an equilibrium is reached (about 1/3 α and 2/3 β).
4. **Oxidation.** Mild oxidation of the aldehyde group gives aldonic acids (glucose → gluconic acid); oxidation of the last carbon gives uronic acids (glucuronic acid, used by the liver to conjugate bilirubin and drugs).
5. **Reduction.** The carbonyl group is reduced to an alcohol: glucose → sorbitol, mannose → mannitol (used as an osmotic diuretic).
6. **Dehydration by strong acids.** Concentrated acids remove water from sugars to give furfural (from pentoses) or hydroxymethylfurfural (from hexoses). These condense with phenols to give coloured products – the basis of Molisch's, Seliwanoff's and Bial's tests.
7. **Glycoside formation.** The anomeric –OH of a sugar joins with an –OH or –NH of another molecule to form a glycoside (for example digoxin is a cardiac glycoside).
8. **Fermentation.** Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide.
9. **Ester formation.** Sugars form phosphate esters, such as glucose-6-phosphate, which are the active forms in metabolism.

## 1.7 Structures of monosaccharides

### Glucose (dextrose, grape sugar)

C6H12O6, an **aldohexose**. It is the main sugar of blood and the main fuel of the brain.

```text
 Open chain (Fischer)          Ring form (Haworth), α-D-glucopyranose

      H–C=O   C1                          CH2OH (C6)
        |                                  |
     H–C–OH   C2                      C5 ──O──
        |                             /         \
    HO–C–H    C3                    C4           C1 ─ OH (α: OH down)
        |                             \         /
     H–C–OH   C4                      C3 ───── C2
        |                             (OH)     (OH)
     H–C–OH   C5   (D-sugar: OH on right at C5)
        |
       CH2OH  C6
```

In water, glucose exists mainly as a six-membered ring (**pyranose**) formed when the –OH on C5 reacts with the aldehyde at C1. C1 then becomes a new chiral centre, called the **anomeric carbon**; this gives α and β forms.

### Fructose (laevulose, fruit sugar)

C6H12O6, a **ketohexose** (keto group at C2). It forms a five-membered ring (**furanose**) in sucrose. It is the sweetest common sugar and is found in fruits, honey and semen.

```text
   Open chain           Haworth (β-D-fructofuranose)
      CH2OH  C1             HOCH2(C6)    O     CH2OH (C1)
      C=O    C2                   \    /   \  /
   HO–C–H    C3                    C5      C2
    H–C–OH   C4                     \       /  \
    H–C–OH   C5                     C4 ── C3    OH
      CH2OH  C6
```

### Galactose

An aldohexose like glucose. It differs from glucose only in the position of the –OH at **C4** (it is the C4 **epimer** of glucose). It comes from lactose of milk and is a part of glycolipids and glycoproteins.

**Epimers** are sugars that differ only in the arrangement around one carbon atom other than the anomeric carbon: glucose and galactose (C4), glucose and mannose (C2).

## 1.8 Structures of disaccharides

| Disaccharide | Units | Linkage | Reducing? | Source / note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Maltose** (malt sugar) | Glucose + glucose | α(1→4) | Yes | Formed when amylase digests starch |
| **Lactose** (milk sugar) | Galactose + glucose | β(1→4) | Yes | Milk; lactase deficiency causes lactose intolerance |
| **Sucrose** (cane sugar, table sugar) | Glucose + fructose | α1 → β2 | No (both anomeric carbons are used in the bond) | Sugar cane, beet; hydrolysis gives "invert sugar" |

```text
 Maltose:   Glc ─α(1→4)─ Glc      (free anomeric C1 on the second glucose → reducing)
 Lactose:   Gal ─β(1→4)─ Glc      (free anomeric C1 on glucose → reducing)
 Sucrose:   Glc ─α1↔β2─ Fru       (no free anomeric carbon → non-reducing)
```

**Invert sugar:** sucrose is dextrorotatory. On hydrolysis (by acid or the enzyme invertase/sucrase) it gives equal amounts of glucose and fructose. Fructose is strongly laevorotatory, so the mixture turns to the left. This change of sign is called inversion, and the mixture is called invert sugar (honey is mostly invert sugar).

## 1.9 Polysaccharides: starch and glycogen

### Starch

The storage carbohydrate of **plants** (rice, wheat, potato, maize). It is a mixture of two glucose polymers.

| Part | Structure | Share | Iodine colour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Amylose** | Long unbranched chain of glucose with α(1→4) bonds; coils into a helix | About 15–20% | Deep blue |
| **Amylopectin** | α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches about every 24–30 glucose units | About 80–85% | Reddish-violet |

Starch gives a blue colour with iodine because iodine fits inside the amylose helix. Starch is not reducing (very few free reducing ends). Amylase hydrolyses it stepwise: starch → dextrins → maltose.

### Glycogen ("animal starch")

The storage carbohydrate of **animals**, stored mainly in the **liver** (keeps blood glucose up between meals) and in **skeletal muscle** (fuel for the muscle itself).

- Made of glucose units with α(1→4) bonds and α(1→6) branches.
- **More branched than amylopectin** – a branch about every 8–12 glucose units. The many branch ends allow fast release of glucose.
- Gives a **red-brown (reddish-violet)** colour with iodine.

```text
 Amylose:      o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o     (straight α1→4)

 Amylopectin:  o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o
                       |  (α1→6)
                       o-o-o-o-o-o         (few branches)

 Glycogen:     o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o
                 |     |     |
                 o-o-o o-o-o o-o-o         (many short branches)
                   |     |
                   o-o   o-o
```

Other polysaccharides worth knowing: **cellulose** (β(1→4) glucose; plant cell walls; humans cannot digest it but it gives dietary fibre), **inulin** (fructose polymer; used to measure GFR), **dextrans** (plasma expanders), **heparin** (anticoagulant), **hyaluronic acid** (joint fluid, used in eye surgery).

## 1.10 Qualitative tests for carbohydrates

| Test | Reagent | Positive result | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Molisch's** | α-naphthol in alcohol + conc. H2SO4 along the side | Violet (purple) ring at the junction | Any carbohydrate (general test) |
| **Iodine** | Dilute iodine solution | Blue (starch); red-brown (glycogen, dextrins) | Polysaccharides |
| **Benedict's** | Alkaline copper sulphate with sodium citrate; boil | Green → yellow → orange → brick-red precipitate | Reducing sugars |
| **Fehling's** | Fehling's A (CuSO4) + Fehling's B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate); boil | Red precipitate of Cu2O | Reducing sugars |
| **Barfoed's** | Copper acetate in acetic acid; boil 2–3 minutes | Brick-red precipitate quickly (within about 2–3 minutes) | Reducing monosaccharides (disaccharides react only after longer heating) |
| **Seliwanoff's** | Resorcinol in HCl; boil | Cherry-red colour quickly | Ketoses (fructose, and sucrose after hydrolysis) |
| **Bial's** | Orcinol in HCl with ferric chloride | Green or blue-green colour | Pentoses |
| **Osazone** | Phenylhydrazine HCl + sodium acetate; boil | Yellow crystals, examined under microscope | Glucose/fructose: needle-shaped (broom-like); maltose: sunflower/petal shaped; lactose: powder-puff or cotton-ball shaped |
| **Fermentation** | Yeast | Gas (CO2) | Fermentable sugars |

```text
 Systematic scheme
 Molisch +  →  Iodine?  blue → starch;  red-brown → glycogen/dextrin
             →  No colour with iodine → Benedict's
                   negative → non-reducing (sucrose: hydrolyse, then Benedict +, Seliwanoff +)
                   positive → Barfoed's
                       quick red → monosaccharide → Seliwanoff (cherry red = fructose)
                                                   → Bial (green = pentose)
                                                   → else glucose/galactose (osazone)
                       late or no red → disaccharide (maltose/lactose: osazone)
```

## 1.11 Biological role of carbohydrates

1. **Main source of energy.** Glucose is oxidised to give ATP; 1 g of carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal. The brain and red blood cells depend on glucose.
2. **Storage of energy** as glycogen (animals) and starch (plants).
3. **Structural role.** Cellulose in plant cell walls; chitin in insects; mucopolysaccharides (chondroitin sulphate, hyaluronic acid) in cartilage, bone and joints.
4. **Components of important molecules:** ribose and deoxyribose in RNA and DNA; ribose in ATP, NAD, FAD and coenzyme A.
5. **Cell recognition and immunity.** Sugar chains on glycoproteins and glycolipids form blood group antigens and receptor sites.
6. **Anticoagulant:** heparin.
7. **Dietary fibre** (cellulose, pectin) helps bowel movement and lowers cholesterol absorption.
8. **Protein sparing:** enough carbohydrate in the diet stops the body from using protein for energy.
9. **Detoxification:** glucuronic acid joins with bilirubin, steroids and many drugs so they can be excreted.
10. **Pharmaceutical uses:** lactose and starch as tablet diluents and disintegrants, sucrose in syrups, dextrose in intravenous fluids, mannitol as an osmotic diuretic.

## Remember

- Biochemistry = chemistry of life; metabolism = all chemical reactions of the body.
- Mitochondria: TCA, β-oxidation, ETC; cytosol: glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis; smooth ER: drug metabolism.
- Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; general formula Cn(H2O)n.
- Glucose = aldohexose (pyranose ring); fructose = ketohexose (furanose ring); galactose = C4 epimer of glucose.
- Maltose Glc-α(1→4)-Glc and lactose Gal-β(1→4)-Glc are reducing; sucrose Glc-α1↔β2-Fru is non-reducing.
- Amylose (unbranched, blue with iodine) + amylopectin (branched) = starch; glycogen is more highly branched (red-brown with iodine).
- Molisch = all carbohydrates; Benedict = reducing; Barfoed = monosaccharides; Seliwanoff = ketoses; Bial = pentoses; iodine = starch.

# Unit 2: Proteins and amino acids

This unit covers syllabus chapter 3 (5 hours).

## 2.1 Definition of proteins

**Proteins** are large organic molecules (macromolecules) made of **α-amino acids** joined together by **peptide bonds**. They contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and **nitrogen** (about 16% by weight); most also contain sulphur, and some contain phosphorus, iron, copper or zinc.

The name comes from the Greek word "proteios", meaning "of first importance". Proteins form enzymes, hormones, antibodies, transport molecules and the structure of the body.

**Peptide bond:** the bond formed between the carboxyl group (–COOH) of one amino acid and the amino group (–NH2) of the next, with the loss of one molecule of water.

```text
   H2N–CH(R1)–COOH  +  H2N–CH(R2)–COOH
                    ↓  (– H2O)
   H2N–CH(R1)–CO–NH–CH(R2)–COOH      a dipeptide
               └──┬──┘
               peptide bond (–CO–NH–)
```

- 2 amino acids = dipeptide; 3 = tripeptide; up to about 10 = oligopeptide; many = polypeptide.
- A chain of more than about 50 amino acids is usually called a protein.
- Every chain has an **N-terminal** end (free –NH2) and a **C-terminal** end (free –COOH).

## 2.2 Amino acids: definition and structure

**Amino acids** are organic compounds that contain an amino group (–NH2) and a carboxyl group (–COOH). In the amino acids of proteins both groups are attached to the same carbon, the **α-carbon**; hence they are called **α-amino acids**.

```text
            R          (side chain – different in each amino acid)
            |
     H2N – Cα – COOH
            |
            H
```

- About **20 standard amino acids** are coded by DNA and found in proteins.
- All except **glycine** (R = H) have a chiral α-carbon, so they are optically active; amino acids of human proteins are of the **L-form**.
- **Zwitterion:** in solution an amino acid carries both a positive (–NH3+) and a negative (–COO−) charge. The pH at which the net charge is zero is the **isoelectric pH (pI)**; at this pH solubility is lowest. This is used to precipitate proteins (for example casein precipitates near pH 4.6).

## 2.3 Classification of amino acids

### A. Based on the chemical nature of the side chain

| Group | Amino acids |
| --- | --- |
| Aliphatic (simple) | Glycine, alanine |
| Branched chain | Valine, leucine, isoleucine |
| Hydroxyl-containing | Serine, threonine (tyrosine also has –OH) |
| Sulphur-containing | Cysteine, methionine |
| Acidic (extra –COOH) and their amides | Aspartic acid, glutamic acid; asparagine, glutamine |
| Basic (extra amino or basic group) | Lysine, arginine, histidine |
| Aromatic (benzene ring) | Phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan |
| Imino acid | Proline (the nitrogen is part of a ring) |

They can also be grouped by **polarity**: non-polar (alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, methionine, tryptophan, proline), polar uncharged (serine, threonine, cysteine, tyrosine, asparagine, glutamine, glycine is often placed here), polar negatively charged (aspartate, glutamate) and polar positively charged (lysine, arginine, histidine).

### B. Based on nutritional requirement

| Type | Meaning | Amino acids |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Essential** (indispensable) | Cannot be made in the body; must come from the diet | Valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, lysine |
| **Semi-essential** | Made in the body but not enough during growth (children, pregnancy) | Arginine, histidine |
| **Non-essential** | Can be made in the body | Glycine, alanine, serine, cysteine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, asparagine, glutamine, tyrosine, proline |

Memory aid for the essential and semi-essential ones: **"PVT TIM HALL"** – Phenylalanine, Valine, Tryptophan, Threonine, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Arginine, Leucine, Lysine. (Many books now count histidine as essential for adults also.)

### C. Based on metabolic fate (useful later in Unit 9)

- **Purely ketogenic:** leucine, lysine (give acetyl CoA or acetoacetate).
- **Both glucogenic and ketogenic:** isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, threonine.
- **Glucogenic:** all the rest (can form glucose).

## 2.4 Classification of proteins

### A. Based on composition

```text
                         Proteins
        ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┐
   Simple proteins    Conjugated proteins    Derived proteins
   (only amino acids) (protein + non-protein  (formed by partial
                       prosthetic group)       breakdown of proteins)
```

**1. Simple proteins** – give only amino acids on hydrolysis (see the solubility table below).

**2. Conjugated (compound) proteins** – a simple protein joined to a non-protein part called the **prosthetic group**.

| Class | Prosthetic group | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glycoproteins | Carbohydrate | Mucin, immunoglobulins, some hormones (FSH, LH) |
| Lipoproteins | Lipid | LDL, HDL, chylomicrons |
| Nucleoproteins | Nucleic acid | Chromatin (DNA + histones), ribosomes |
| Phosphoproteins | Phosphoric acid | Casein (milk), vitellin (egg yolk) |
| Chromoproteins | Coloured pigment | Haemoglobin (haem), cytochromes, rhodopsin |
| Metalloproteins | Metal ion | Ceruloplasmin (copper), ferritin (iron), carbonic anhydrase (zinc) |

**3. Derived proteins**

- **Primary derived proteins** (slight change, little hydrolysis): coagulated proteins (cooked egg white), proteans, metaproteins.
- **Secondary derived proteins** (more hydrolysis, smaller pieces): proteoses → peptones → peptides.

### B. Based on solubility (classes of simple proteins)

| Class | Soluble in | Coagulated by heat? | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Albumins** | Water and dilute salt solutions | Yes | Serum albumin, egg albumin (ovalbumin), lactalbumin |
| **Globulins** | Dilute salt solutions; insoluble in pure water | Yes | Serum globulins, immunoglobulins, myosin, ovoglobulin |
| **Glutelins** | Dilute acids and alkalis | Yes | Glutenin (wheat), oryzenin (rice) |
| **Prolamines** | 70–80% alcohol | No | Gliadin (wheat), zein (maize) |
| **Histones** | Water and dilute acids; basic proteins | No | Proteins bound to DNA in chromatin |
| **Protamines** | Water; strongly basic, small | No | Salmine (salmon sperm); protamine sulphate is used to reverse heparin |
| **Scleroproteins (albuminoids)** | Insoluble in most solvents; fibrous | No | Keratin (hair, nails), collagen (skin, bone, tendon), elastin |

### C. Based on shape

- **Fibrous proteins:** long, thread-like, insoluble, structural – keratin, collagen, elastin, fibrin.
- **Globular proteins:** compact, round, soluble, functional – enzymes, haemoglobin, albumin, insulin, antibodies.

## 2.5 Structure of proteins: four levels of organisation

```text
 Primary      ─ Ala─Gly─Ser─Leu─Lys─...      (sequence)
 Secondary    ─ α-helix  ⌇⌇⌇⌇   or β-sheet  ⇉⇉⇉   (local H-bonded shape)
 Tertiary     ─ whole chain folded into a 3-D shape  (◯)
 Quaternary   ─ several folded chains packed together (◯◯/◯◯ e.g. haemoglobin)
```

### Primary structure

- The **sequence** (order) of amino acids in the polypeptide chain, from the N-terminal to the C-terminal end.
- Held by **peptide bonds** (covalent); disulphide bonds also belong here.
- It is decided by the gene and it decides all higher levels. A single change can cause disease: in **sickle cell anaemia**, glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-chain of haemoglobin is replaced by valine.
- Insulin was the first protein whose sequence was found (Frederick Sanger): two chains, A (21 amino acids) and B (30), linked by disulphide bonds.

### Secondary structure

The regular, local folding of the chain, held by **hydrogen bonds** between the C=O and N–H of peptide bonds.

- **α-helix:** a right-handed coil; hydrogen bonds run along the axis between each C=O and the N–H four residues ahead; about 3.6 amino acids per turn. Found in keratin and in parts of most globular proteins (myoglobin is mostly α-helix). Proline breaks the helix.
- **β-pleated sheet:** extended chains lying side by side, joined by hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains; can be parallel or antiparallel. Found in silk fibroin.
- **Collagen** has its own special **triple helix** (three chains wound together; glycine at every third position).

### Tertiary structure

The overall **three-dimensional folding** of one complete polypeptide chain. Held by bonds between side chains:

| Bond | Formed between |
| --- | --- |
| Disulphide bonds (covalent, strongest) | Two cysteine –SH groups |
| Hydrogen bonds | Polar side chains |
| Ionic bonds (salt bridges) | Positively and negatively charged side chains (lysine and aspartate) |
| Hydrophobic interactions | Non-polar side chains, which hide inside the protein, away from water |
| Van der Waals forces | Close atoms |

The active site of an enzyme and the binding site of a receptor are formed at this level. Myoglobin is a single chain with only tertiary structure.

### Quaternary structure

The arrangement of **two or more polypeptide chains (subunits)** into one functional protein, held by the same non-covalent bonds (sometimes disulphide bonds). Example: **haemoglobin** = 2 α + 2 β chains (a tetramer); lactate dehydrogenase (4 subunits); immunoglobulin G (2 heavy + 2 light chains).

### Denaturation

**Denaturation** is the loss of the natural (native) secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, without breaking peptide bonds. The protein loses its biological activity.

- Causes: heat, strong acids and alkalis, heavy metal salts (Hg, Pb, Ag), alcohol, urea, detergents, UV light, vigorous shaking.
- Effects: decreased solubility, loss of enzyme or hormone activity, easier digestion (cooked egg).
- Usually irreversible; sometimes reversible (renaturation).
- Practical uses: sterilisation by heat and alcohol; heavy metal poisoning is treated with egg white or milk, which bind the metal.

## 2.6 Qualitative tests for proteins and amino acids

| Test | Reagent | Positive result | Detects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Biuret** | NaOH + dilute CuSO4 | Violet / purple colour | Peptide bonds (proteins and peptides with 2 or more peptide bonds); not given by free amino acids |
| **Ninhydrin** | Ninhydrin; boil | Purple (Ruhemann's purple); proline and hydroxyproline give yellow | Free α-amino groups – all amino acids and proteins |
| **Xanthoproteic** | Conc. HNO3, heat; then add NaOH/ammonia | Yellow, turning orange with alkali | Aromatic amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan; phenylalanine weakly) |
| **Millon's** | Mercuric sulphate in H2SO4 + sodium nitrite; warm | Red precipitate or colour | Tyrosine (phenolic –OH) |
| **Hopkins–Cole (glyoxylic acid)** | Glyoxylic acid + conc. H2SO4 along the side | Violet ring | Tryptophan (indole ring) |
| **Sulphur (lead acetate)** | Strong NaOH, boil, then lead acetate | Black precipitate (lead sulphide) | Cysteine / cystine (not methionine) |
| **Sakaguchi** | α-naphthol + sodium hypobromite in alkali | Red colour | Arginine (guanidino group) |
| **Heat coagulation** | Heat, then a drop of acetic acid | White coagulum | Albumins and globulins |
| **Precipitation tests** | Heavy metals, alkaloidal reagents (picric acid, tannic acid), alcohol, salting out with ammonium sulphate | Precipitate | Proteins in general |

**Salting out:** globulins precipitate at half saturation with ammonium sulphate; albumins only at full saturation. This separates the two.

## 2.7 Biological role of proteins and amino acids

**Proteins**

1. **Catalytic:** all enzymes are proteins (amylase, pepsin, DNA polymerase).
2. **Structural:** collagen, keratin, elastin.
3. **Transport:** haemoglobin (oxygen), albumin (drugs, fatty acids, bilirubin), transferrin (iron), lipoproteins (lipids).
4. **Hormones:** insulin, growth hormone, glucagon, oxytocin.
5. **Defence:** antibodies (immunoglobulins), complement proteins, fibrinogen and other clotting factors.
6. **Contraction and movement:** actin, myosin.
7. **Storage:** ferritin (iron), casein (milk), ovalbumin.
8. **Receptors and signalling:** cell surface receptors, ion channels.
9. **Regulation:** maintain colloid osmotic pressure of plasma (albumin) and act as buffers (haemoglobin, plasma proteins).
10. **Energy:** 1 g protein gives about 4 kcal, used mainly in starvation.

**Amino acids** (besides building proteins)

| Amino acid | Important product |
| --- | --- |
| Tyrosine | Thyroxine, adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, melanin |
| Tryptophan | Serotonin, melatonin, niacin |
| Histidine | Histamine |
| Glutamate | GABA (inhibitory neurotransmitter) |
| Glycine | Haem, creatine, glutathione, bile salt conjugation |
| Arginine | Nitric oxide, creatine, urea |
| Methionine | S-adenosylmethionine (methyl donor) |
| Cysteine | Glutathione (antioxidant), taurine |

## 2.8 Diseases related to malnutrition of proteins

**Protein–energy malnutrition (PEM)**, now often called protein–energy undernutrition, is common in young children in developing countries, especially after weaning. Its two extreme forms are kwashiorkor and marasmus.

| Feature | Kwashiorkor | Marasmus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main cause | Lack of protein with fairly adequate calories (weaned onto a starchy diet) | Lack of both protein and calories (near starvation) |
| Usual age | 1–4 years | Below 1 year |
| Oedema | **Present** (low plasma albumin lowers oncotic pressure) | Absent |
| Body weight | 60–80% of expected (oedema hides wasting) | Below 60% of expected; severe wasting |
| Subcutaneous fat | Partly preserved | Lost – "skin and bones", old-man face |
| Face | Moon face | Shrunken, old-looking |
| Liver | Enlarged **fatty liver** (no protein to make lipoproteins that export fat) | Not fatty |
| Skin | "Flaky paint" dermatitis, depigmentation | Dry, loose, wrinkled |
| Hair | Thin, sparse, brittle, reddish (flag sign) | Mostly normal |
| Appetite and mood | Poor appetite, apathy, irritable | Good appetite, alert |
| Plasma albumin | Very low | Normal or slightly low |

**Marasmic kwashiorkor** shows features of both. Other effects of protein deficiency: poor growth, anaemia, low immunity (frequent infections), poor wound healing and delayed mental development.

**Treatment and prevention:** correct dehydration and infection first, then feed slowly with a balanced, energy- and protein-rich diet; promote breast-feeding, proper weaning foods, nutrition programmes (ICDS, mid-day meals) and health education.

**Recommended intake:** commonly quoted as about **0.8–1 g of good-quality protein per kg body weight per day** for adults, more in growing children, pregnancy and lactation.

## Remember

- Proteins are polymers of L-α-amino acids joined by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–); nitrogen about 16%.
- Essential amino acids: PVT TIM HALL (histidine and arginine semi-essential); leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
- Simple, conjugated (prosthetic group) and derived proteins; by solubility: albumins (water), globulins (dilute salt), glutelins (dilute acid/alkali), prolamines (70–80% alcohol), histones, protamines, scleroproteins (insoluble).
- Primary = sequence (peptide bonds); secondary = α-helix and β-sheet (H-bonds); tertiary = 3-D fold (side-chain bonds); quaternary = subunits (haemoglobin).
- Biuret = peptide bonds; ninhydrin = α-amino groups; xanthoproteic = aromatic; Millon's = tyrosine; Hopkins–Cole = tryptophan; lead acetate = cysteine; Sakaguchi = arginine.
- Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency, oedema, fatty liver; marasmus: protein + energy deficiency, severe wasting, no oedema.

# Unit 3: Lipids

This unit covers syllabus chapter 4 (5 hours).

## 3.1 Definition

**Lipids** are a group of naturally occurring organic compounds that are **insoluble (or poorly soluble) in water** and **soluble in non-polar (fat) solvents** such as chloroform, ether, benzene and acetone. They are esters of fatty acids with alcohols, or substances related to them, and they can be used by living organisms.

Lipids include fats, oils, waxes, phospholipids, steroids (cholesterol) and the fat-soluble vitamins. Because they do not dissolve in water, they are carried in blood as **lipoproteins**.

## 3.2 Classification of lipids (Bloor's classification)

```text
                              Lipids
        ┌───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
  Simple lipids            Compound lipids          Derived lipids
  (fatty acid + alcohol)   (simple lipid +          (obtained by hydrolysis
                            another group)           of the first two)
  ├ Fats and oils          ├ Phospholipids           ├ Fatty acids
  │ (triglycerides)        ├ Glycolipids             ├ Glycerol and other alcohols
  └ Waxes                  ├ Lipoproteins            ├ Steroids (cholesterol)
                           └ Others (sulpholipids,   ├ Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K
                             aminolipids)            ├ Ketone bodies
                                                     └ Eicosanoids (prostaglandins)
```

### 1. Simple lipids

Esters of fatty acids with alcohols.

- **Fats and oils (triacylglycerols, triglycerides):** esters of fatty acids with **glycerol**. Fats are solid at room temperature (butter, ghee, lard); oils are liquid (groundnut, sunflower, mustard oil).
- **Waxes:** esters of fatty acids with **long-chain monohydric alcohols** (not glycerol). Examples: beeswax, spermaceti, lanolin (wool fat), carnauba wax. Uses: ointment bases, tablet coating, polishes.

### 2. Compound (conjugated) lipids

Esters of fatty acids and alcohol that also contain another group.

| Class | Extra group | Examples | Where / role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Phospholipids** (glycerophospholipids) | Phosphoric acid + a base | **Lecithin** (phosphatidylcholine), **cephalin** (phosphatidylethanolamine), phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol | Cell membranes; lecithin in lung surfactant (as dipalmitoyl lecithin) and as an emulsifier |
| Phospholipids (sphingophospholipids) | Sphingosine instead of glycerol | **Sphingomyelin** | Myelin sheath of nerves |
| **Glycolipids** | Carbohydrate + sphingosine | **Cerebrosides**, **gangliosides** | Brain and nerve tissue; cell recognition |
| **Lipoproteins** | Protein | Chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL, HDL | Transport of lipids in blood |

### 3. Derived lipids

Formed by hydrolysis of simple and compound lipids, but still having lipid properties: fatty acids, glycerol, **steroids** (cholesterol, bile acids, sex hormones), fat-soluble vitamins, ketone bodies, and **eicosanoids** (prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, made from arachidonic acid).

**Amphipathic lipids:** molecules with both a water-loving (polar head) and a water-hating (non-polar tail) part, such as phospholipids, cholesterol and bile salts. They form membranes, micelles and liposomes and act as emulsifiers.

## 3.3 Triglycerides (oils and fats): structure

A triglyceride is formed when the three –OH groups of glycerol are esterified with three fatty acids.

```text
   CH2–OH        HOOC–R1          CH2–O–CO–R1
   |                              |
   CH–OH    +    HOOC–R2   ──→    CH–O–CO–R2     +  3 H2O
   |                              |
   CH2–OH        HOOC–R3          CH2–O–CO–R3
  Glycerol    3 fatty acids      Triacylglycerol (triglyceride)
```

- **Simple triglyceride:** all three fatty acids are the same (tripalmitin, triolein).
- **Mixed triglyceride:** different fatty acids – most natural fats and oils.
- Triglycerides are **neutral fats** (no charge) and are the main **stored energy** of the body (adipose tissue). 1 g of fat gives about **9 kcal**, more than double that of carbohydrate or protein.
- Fats are rich in saturated fatty acids (solid); oils are rich in unsaturated fatty acids (liquid, lower melting point).

## 3.4 Properties of triglycerides

### Physical properties

- Colourless, odourless and tasteless when pure; natural colour comes from pigments such as carotenes.
- Insoluble in water, soluble in fat solvents; lighter than water (float).
- Leave a **translucent grease spot** on paper.
- Form **emulsions** with water in the presence of emulsifiers (bile salts, soaps, proteins).

### Chemical properties

1. **Hydrolysis:** by lipases (in the gut, pancreatic lipase), acids or superheated steam → glycerol + fatty acids.
2. **Saponification:** hydrolysis by an alkali (NaOH or KOH) gives glycerol and **soaps** (sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids).

   ```text
   Triglyceride + 3 NaOH  →  Glycerol + 3 R–COONa (soap)
   ```

3. **Hydrogenation:** hydrogen is added across double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids using a nickel catalyst, turning liquid oils into solid fats (vanaspati). Partial hydrogenation forms **trans fatty acids**, which raise LDL-cholesterol and the risk of heart disease.
4. **Halogenation:** iodine adds to double bonds – the basis of the iodine value.
5. **Rancidity:** the unpleasant smell and taste of fats on storage.
   - **Hydrolytic rancidity:** lipases from microbes release short-chain fatty acids (butyric acid in butter) – helped by moisture and warmth.
   - **Oxidative rancidity:** oxygen attacks double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids forming peroxides, aldehydes and ketones – helped by light, heat and metals.
   - Prevention: store in cool, dark, airtight containers; add **antioxidants** such as vitamin E (tocopherol), BHA, BHT and propyl gallate.
6. **Acrolein formation:** heating glycerol (or a fat) with potassium bisulphate removes water and gives acrolein, which has a sharp, irritating smell.

### Constants used to test fats and oils

| Constant | Definition | What it tells |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Saponification value** | mg of KOH needed to saponify 1 g of fat | Average chain length – higher value means shorter chains (lower molecular weight) |
| **Iodine value** | g of iodine absorbed by 100 g of fat | Degree of unsaturation – higher in oils |
| **Acid value** | mg of KOH needed to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 g of fat | Free fatty acids – rises with hydrolytic rancidity |
| **Peroxide value** | Amount of peroxides present (milliequivalents of peroxide per kg) | Oxidative rancidity |
| **Reichert–Meissl number** | ml of 0.1 N alkali needed to neutralise the volatile, water-soluble fatty acids from 5 g of fat | Short-chain fatty acids; used to detect adulteration of butter and ghee |

## 3.5 Fatty acids

**Fatty acids** are long-chain carboxylic acids, R–COOH. Natural fatty acids usually have an **even number of carbon atoms** (made from 2-carbon units) and are unbranched.

### A. Classification based on chemical nature

**1. By saturation**

| Type | Double bonds | Examples (carbon atoms : double bonds) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Saturated** | None | Butyric (4:0, in butter), palmitic (16:0), stearic (18:0) |
| **Monounsaturated (MUFA)** | One | Oleic acid (18:1) – olive, groundnut oil; palmitoleic (16:1) |
| **Polyunsaturated (PUFA)** | Two or more | Linoleic (18:2, ω-6), α-linolenic (18:3, ω-3), arachidonic (20:4, ω-6), EPA (20:5, ω-3) and DHA (22:6, ω-3) from fish oils |

**2. By chain length:** short chain (2–6 carbons, e.g. butyric), medium chain (8–12, e.g. coconut oil acids), long chain (14 or more, e.g. palmitic, stearic, oleic).

**3. By position of the first double bond from the methyl end:** omega-3 (α-linolenic, EPA, DHA), omega-6 (linoleic, arachidonic), omega-9 (oleic).

**4. Cis and trans:** natural unsaturated fatty acids are mostly **cis** (bent chain); **trans** fats form during partial hydrogenation and are harmful.

### B. Classification based on nutritional requirement

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Essential fatty acids (EFA)** | Cannot be made in the body because humans cannot put a double bond beyond carbon 9; must come from the diet | **Linoleic acid** (ω-6) and **α-linolenic acid** (ω-3) |
| Conditionally (semi-) essential | Made from linoleic acid, so needed in the diet only if linoleic acid is short | **Arachidonic acid** |
| Non-essential | Made in the body | Palmitic, stearic, oleic acid |

**Functions of essential fatty acids:** parts of membrane phospholipids; precursors of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes; lower blood cholesterol; needed for healthy skin and for brain and retina development (DHA).

**EFA deficiency:** rough, scaly skin (phrynoderma, "toad skin"), hair loss, poor wound healing, poor growth; seen in long-term fat-free parenteral nutrition. Sources: vegetable oils (sunflower, safflower, soybean), fish, flaxseed, nuts.

## 3.6 Cholesterol: structure and functions

**Cholesterol** is the most important **sterol** of animals. It is a derived lipid; it is **not found in plants** (plants contain phytosterols).

### Structure

- Formula C27H46O (**27 carbon atoms**).
- Built on the **cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene** (steroid) nucleus: four fused rings A, B, C (six-membered) and D (five-membered).
- An **–OH group at carbon 3** (so it is an alcohol), a **double bond between carbons 5 and 6**, two methyl groups (C18, C19) and an **8-carbon side chain at carbon 17**.

```text
 Sketch of cholesterol (rings drawn as boxes)

                          CH3 (C18)   8-carbon side chain
                            |        /
                     ┌──────┴──┐  ┌─┴──┐
          CH3 (C19)  │ ring C  ├──┤ D  │  ← C17 (ring D has 5 carbons)
              |      │ (6 C)   │  └────┘
       ┌──────┴──┬───┴─────────┘
       │ ring A  │ ring B  │
 HO ── │ (C3)    │ C5=C6   │    rings A, B, C have 6 carbons each
       └─────────┴─────────┘
```

- In blood about two-thirds of cholesterol is in the **esterified** form (a fatty acid attached at C3); it is carried mainly in **LDL**.
- Sources: diet (egg yolk, meat, liver, butter, ghee) and synthesis in the body, mainly in the **liver**, from **acetyl CoA**. The key (rate-limiting) enzyme is **HMG-CoA reductase**, which is blocked by **statins**.

### Functions of cholesterol

1. **Cell membranes:** an essential part of the plasma membrane; it controls membrane fluidity.
2. **Bile acids and bile salts:** made from cholesterol in the liver; needed for fat digestion and absorption. This is also the main route by which the body gets rid of cholesterol.
3. **Steroid hormones:** cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone are all made from cholesterol.
4. **Vitamin D3:** 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin is converted to cholecalciferol by sunlight (UV rays).
5. **Nerve tissue:** present in large amounts in brain and myelin, helping nerve insulation.
6. **Skin:** helps make skin waterproof.

**Clinical point:** high blood cholesterol (especially LDL) leads to **atherosclerosis** – fatty plaques in arteries – causing coronary heart disease and stroke (see Units 8 and 11). Desirable total serum cholesterol is commonly quoted as below about 200 mg/dl; ranges vary by laboratory.

## 3.7 Lipoproteins

Lipids are insoluble in water, so they travel in blood packed inside **lipoproteins**: spherical particles with a **core** of triglycerides and cholesterol esters and a **surface** of phospholipids, free cholesterol and proteins called **apolipoproteins (apoproteins)**.

```text
        Surface: phospholipids, free cholesterol, apoproteins
            ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○
          ○               ○
         ○   CORE: TG +     ○
         ○   cholesterol    ○
          ○    esters      ○
            ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○
```

### Types, composition and functions

Lipoproteins are separated by **ultracentrifugation** (by density) or electrophoresis. The more triglyceride a particle carries, the larger and lighter it is.

| Lipoprotein | Made in | Main lipid carried | Main apoproteins | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Chylomicrons** | Intestine | Dietary triglycerides (about 85–90%) | B-48, C-II, E | Carry **dietary (exogenous)** fat from the intestine to tissues; largest and lightest |
| **VLDL** (very low density) | Liver | Triglycerides made in the liver | B-100, C-II, E | Carry **endogenous** triglycerides from the liver to tissues |
| **IDL** (intermediate density) | Formed from VLDL in blood | Triglycerides and cholesterol | B-100, E | Short-lived; changes to LDL |
| **LDL** (low density) | Formed from IDL | **Cholesterol** (richest) | B-100 | Carry cholesterol **to the tissues**; excess deposits in artery walls – "**bad cholesterol**" |
| **HDL** (high density) | Liver and intestine | Protein-rich; phospholipids and cholesterol | A-I, A-II, C, E | Carry cholesterol **from tissues back to the liver** (reverse cholesterol transport) – "**good cholesterol**"; smallest and densest |

**Lipoprotein lipase** (on the walls of blood capillaries) breaks down the triglycerides of chylomicrons and VLDL; apo C-II activates it. LDL is taken up by cells through **LDL receptors** (recognising apo B-100); a genetic defect of these receptors causes **familial hypercholesterolaemia**.

```text
 Intestine → Chylomicrons → (LPL) → remnants → liver
 Liver → VLDL → (LPL) → IDL → LDL → tissues (LDL receptor)
 Tissues → cholesterol → HDL → liver → bile acids → excreted
```

## 3.8 Qualitative tests for lipids

| Test | Method | Positive result | Detects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Solubility** | Shake with water, alcohol and chloroform | Insoluble in water, soluble in chloroform/ether | Lipids in general |
| **Translucent spot (grease spot)** | Put a drop on filter paper and let dry | Permanent translucent spot | Fats and oils |
| **Emulsification** | Shake oil with water, then with bile salt or soap solution | Stable emulsion only with the emulsifier | Emulsifying action |
| **Saponification** | Boil with alcoholic KOH, add water and shake | Froth (soap formed) | Fats and oils (esters) |
| **Acrolein** | Heat with solid potassium bisulphate (KHSO4) | Sharp, irritating smell of acrolein | Glycerol (free or in fats) |
| **Sudan III / IV** | Add a few drops of Sudan dye, shake with water | Red-coloured oil layer | Fats |
| **Unsaturation (Hübl's iodine)** | Add iodine solution drop by drop | Colour of iodine disappears | Unsaturated fatty acids |
| **Salkowski** | Cholesterol in chloroform + conc. H2SO4 along the side | Red colour in the upper chloroform layer, yellow-green fluorescence in the acid layer | Cholesterol |
| **Liebermann–Burchard** | Cholesterol in chloroform + acetic anhydride + conc. H2SO4 | Red → blue → **green** colour | Cholesterol (also basis of an old quantitative method) |

## 3.9 Functions of lipids

1. **Energy store:** triglycerides in adipose tissue are the largest energy reserve; 1 g gives about 9 kcal.
2. **Structural:** phospholipids and cholesterol form cell membranes.
3. **Insulation and protection:** subcutaneous fat keeps body heat; fat around kidneys and other organs protects them from injury.
4. **Nerve function:** myelin (sphingomyelin, glycolipids) insulates nerve fibres for fast conduction.
5. **Carriers of fat-soluble vitamins** A, D, E and K; dietary fat is needed for their absorption.
6. **Precursors:** cholesterol → steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D; arachidonic acid → prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes.
7. **Emulsifiers and surfactants:** bile salts in fat digestion; lung surfactant (dipalmitoyl lecithin) prevents collapse of alveoli – its lack causes respiratory distress syndrome in premature babies.
8. **Signalling:** phosphatidylinositol gives second messengers (IP3, DAG).
9. **Pharmaceutical uses:** oils and fats as vehicles and ointment bases (arachis oil, wool fat, beeswax); lecithin as an emulsifier; phospholipids in liposomes.

## Remember

- Lipids: insoluble in water, soluble in fat solvents; esters of fatty acids with alcohols.
- Bloor: simple (fats, oils, waxes), compound (phospholipids, glycolipids, lipoproteins), derived (fatty acids, steroids, fat-soluble vitamins).
- Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids; saponification value → chain length; iodine value → unsaturation; acid value → free fatty acids.
- Essential fatty acids: linoleic (ω-6) and α-linolenic (ω-3); arachidonic is semi-essential.
- Cholesterol: 27 C, steroid nucleus, –OH at C3, double bond C5–C6; makes bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D3; HMG-CoA reductase is its key enzyme.
- Chylomicrons (dietary TG), VLDL (liver TG), LDL ("bad", cholesterol to tissues), HDL ("good", cholesterol back to liver).
- Acrolein test = glycerol; Salkowski and Liebermann–Burchard = cholesterol.

# Unit 4: Nucleic acids and introduction to biotechnology

This unit covers syllabus chapter 5 (nucleic acids, 4 hours) and chapter 11 (introduction to biotechnology, 1 hour). They are joined here because biotechnology is built directly on DNA and RNA.

## 4.1 Definition of nucleic acids

**Nucleic acids** are long-chain polymers of **nucleotides** joined by **3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds**. They store and transfer genetic information and direct the synthesis of proteins.

There are two types:

- **DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid):** the genetic material; found mainly in the nucleus (also in mitochondria).
- **RNA (ribonucleic acid):** helps to express the genetic information as proteins; found in the nucleus and cytoplasm.

They were first isolated from pus cells by Friedrich Miescher (1869), who called them "nuclein".

## 4.2 Components of nucleic acids

Each nucleotide has three parts:

```text
   Nitrogenous base  +  Pentose sugar  +  Phosphate
   (purine or           (ribose in RNA,
    pyrimidine)          deoxyribose in DNA)

   Base + sugar                 = NUCLEOSIDE
   Base + sugar + phosphate     = NUCLEOTIDE
   Many nucleotides joined      = NUCLEIC ACID (polynucleotide)
```

### Purine and pyrimidine bases

| Group | Ring structure | Bases | Found in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Purines** | Two fused rings (a six-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring) | **Adenine (A)**, **Guanine (G)** | Both DNA and RNA |
| **Pyrimidines** | Single six-membered ring with two nitrogens | **Cytosine (C)** | Both DNA and RNA |
| | | **Thymine (T)** (5-methyluracil) | DNA only |
| | | **Uracil (U)** | RNA only |

```text
   Purine (two rings)              Pyrimidine (one ring)
        N                                N
      /   \   N                        /   \
     |     |--- \                     |     |
     |     |    /  (imidazole)        |     |
      \   /   N                        \   /
        N                                N
     6-membered + 5-membered          6-membered
```

**Minor and related bases:** hypoxanthine and xanthine (formed during purine breakdown), 5-methylcytosine, dihydrouracil and pseudouridine (in tRNA). **Uric acid** is the end product of purine breakdown in humans; excess causes **gout**.

**Drugs that are base analogues:** 5-fluorouracil, 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine (anticancer/immunosuppressant); allopurinol (a hypoxanthine analogue that blocks xanthine oxidase in gout); acyclovir and zidovudine (antiviral nucleoside analogues).

### Pentose sugar

- **D-ribose** in RNA.
- **2-deoxy-D-ribose** in DNA (no –OH at carbon 2′).
- Carbons of the sugar are numbered with a prime (1′ to 5′) to separate them from the atoms of the base.

## 4.3 Nucleosides and nucleotides

### Nucleosides

A **nucleoside** = base + pentose sugar, joined by a **β-N-glycosidic bond** between C1′ of the sugar and N9 of a purine or N1 of a pyrimidine.

| Base | Ribonucleoside | Deoxyribonucleoside |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adenine | Adenosine | Deoxyadenosine |
| Guanine | Guanosine | Deoxyguanosine |
| Cytosine | Cytidine | Deoxycytidine |
| Uracil | Uridine | – |
| Thymine | – | Thymidine (deoxythymidine) |

### Nucleotides

A **nucleotide** = nucleoside + one or more **phosphate** groups, usually esterified at C5′ of the sugar. They are the building blocks of nucleic acids and also have important free roles.

| Nucleotide | Function |
| --- | --- |
| **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) | Energy currency of the cell; two high-energy phosphate bonds |
| ADP, AMP | Formed when ATP is used; regulate metabolism |
| **cAMP** (cyclic AMP) | Second messenger for hormones such as adrenaline and glucagon |
| cGMP | Second messenger (nitric oxide action, vision) |
| GTP | Energy for protein synthesis; signalling through G-proteins |
| UTP / UDP-glucose | Glycogen synthesis |
| CTP / CDP-choline | Phospholipid synthesis |
| **NAD+, NADP+** | Coenzymes of dehydrogenases (contain AMP and niacin) |
| **FAD** | Coenzyme of flavoproteins (contains AMP and riboflavin) |
| **Coenzyme A** | Carries acyl groups (contains ADP and pantothenic acid) |
| S-adenosylmethionine | Methyl group donor |

```text
   Adenine
     │ (N9 – C1′ glycosidic bond)
   Ribose ──C5′–O–P–O–P–O–P          ATP
                α   β   γ
              (β and γ bonds are high-energy)
```

## 4.4 Structure of DNA: the Watson and Crick model

James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the **double helix** model of DNA in **1953**, using the X-ray diffraction pictures of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins and the base-ratio rules of Erwin Chargaff.

### Features of the Watson–Crick (B-form) model

1. DNA is made of **two polynucleotide strands** wound around a common axis to form a **right-handed double helix**.
2. The two strands are **antiparallel**: one runs 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′.
3. The **sugar–phosphate backbone** lies on the outside; the **bases** lie inside, stacked flat, at right angles to the axis.
4. Bases of the two strands pair by **hydrogen bonds** according to the **complementary base-pairing rule**:
   - **A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds** (A=T)
   - **G pairs with C by three hydrogen bonds** (G≡C)
   - A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so the width of the helix is constant.
5. Therefore, in any double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C, and total purines = total pyrimidines (**Chargaff's rule**). GC-rich DNA is more stable (melts at a higher temperature).
6. Dimensions: diameter about **2 nm (20 Å)**; one complete turn every **3.4 nm (34 Å)**; about **10 base pairs per turn**; distance between neighbouring base pairs **0.34 nm (3.4 Å)**.
7. The helix has a **major groove** and a **minor groove**, where proteins (like transcription factors) can bind.
8. The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds and base stacking; they separate on heating (**denaturation / melting**) and join again on cooling (**renaturation / annealing**).

```text
     5′  3′
     │    │      Sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside
     A ═══ T     2 H-bonds
     G ≡≡≡ C     3 H-bonds
     T ═══ A
     C ≡≡≡ G
     │    │
     3′  5′      antiparallel strands, right-handed twist,
                 10 base pairs per turn, 3.4 nm per turn
```

Other forms: **A-DNA** (right-handed, shorter and wider, in dehydrated DNA) and **Z-DNA** (left-handed, zig-zag backbone).

### Functions of DNA

1. Stores the **genetic information** (the genes) in the sequence of its bases.
2. **Replication:** makes an exact copy of itself before cell division (semi-conservative), so the information passes to daughter cells and offspring.
3. **Transcription:** acts as a template for RNA synthesis, controlling protein synthesis and all cell activities.
4. **Mutation** (change in base sequence) is the basis of variation and evolution, and also of genetic disease and cancer.

**Central dogma of molecular biology:**

```text
         replication
        ┌────────┐
        ▼        │
       DNA ──────┘ ── transcription ──▶ RNA ── translation ──▶ Protein
                        (reverse transcription in retroviruses: RNA → DNA)
```

## 4.5 Structure and types of RNA

RNA differs from DNA in:

| Feature | DNA | RNA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sugar | Deoxyribose | Ribose |
| Bases | A, G, C, **T** | A, G, C, **U** |
| Strands | Double-stranded helix | Usually single-stranded (folds back on itself to form hairpin loops) |
| Chargaff's rule | Followed | Not followed |
| Location | Mainly nucleus | Nucleus and cytoplasm |
| Stability | Stable (long-lived) | Less stable; easily hydrolysed by alkali |
| Function | Stores genetic information | Expresses it as protein |

### Types of RNA

| Type | Share of cell RNA | Structure | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **mRNA** (messenger) | About 5% | Linear; 5′ **cap** (7-methylguanosine) and 3′ **poly-A tail** in eukaryotes | Carries the genetic **message** (codons) from DNA to ribosomes; each **codon** of 3 bases codes one amino acid |
| **tRNA** (transfer) | About 15% | Small (about 75–90 nucleotides); **cloverleaf** shape (L-shaped in 3-D); has an **anticodon** loop and a **CCA** end that carries the amino acid; has unusual bases | **Carries amino acids** to the ribosome and reads the codon through its anticodon (an "adaptor") |
| **rRNA** (ribosomal) | About 80% | Folded, combined with proteins to form ribosomes | Forms the structure of **ribosomes**; one rRNA acts as an enzyme (peptidyl transferase) that forms peptide bonds |
| Small RNAs (snRNA, miRNA, siRNA) | Small | Short chains | Splicing of mRNA, gene silencing |

```text
 tRNA (cloverleaf)            CCA–3′ (amino acid attaches here)
                               │
              D-loop  ○──┤acceptor stem├──○  TψC loop
                          │
                       anticodon loop
                         (e.g. reads codon on mRNA)
```

**Genetic code:** 64 codons; 61 code amino acids and 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG is the start codon (methionine). The code is universal (with small exceptions), non-overlapping and degenerate (more than one codon for most amino acids).

## 4.6 Introduction to biotechnology

**Biotechnology** is the use of living organisms, cells or their parts (such as enzymes and genes) to make products or processes useful to humans.

- **Traditional biotechnology:** fermentation to make curd, bread, alcohol, vinegar, antibiotics (penicillin), vitamins and enzymes.
- **Modern biotechnology:** recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering), hybridoma technology (monoclonal antibodies), cell and tissue culture, gene therapy, PCR, genomics.

### Recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering)

Joining a gene from one organism with the DNA of another so that the host makes the product of that gene.

```text
 1. Isolate the wanted gene (e.g. human insulin gene)
 2. Cut the gene and a vector (plasmid) with the same RESTRICTION ENZYME
 3. Join them with DNA LIGASE → recombinant DNA
 4. Put recombinant DNA into a host cell (E. coli or yeast) → TRANSFORMATION
 5. Select the transformed cells (antibiotic-resistance marker)
 6. Grow them in a fermenter → host makes the protein
 7. Extract and purify the product (downstream processing)
```

| Tool | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Restriction endonucleases** ("molecular scissors") | Cut DNA at specific base sequences (e.g. EcoRI) |
| **DNA ligase** ("molecular glue") | Joins DNA pieces |
| **Vectors** | Carry the gene into the host: plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids, viral vectors |
| **Host cells** | E. coli, yeast, mammalian cells (such as CHO cells) |
| **PCR (polymerase chain reaction)** | Makes millions of copies of a DNA segment using a heat-stable (Taq) DNA polymerase; used in diagnosis (COVID-19 RT-PCR, HIV, TB), forensics |

### Products and applications in pharmacy

| Area | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Hormones | Human insulin (the first recombinant drug, approved 1982), insulin analogues, growth hormone |
| Blood products | Erythropoietin (anaemia of kidney failure), clotting factor VIII (haemophilia), tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase) |
| Immune modulators | Interferons (hepatitis, some cancers), interleukins, filgrastim (G-CSF) |
| Vaccines | Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine (surface antigen made in yeast), HPV vaccine |
| Monoclonal antibodies | Made by **hybridoma technology** (Köhler and Milstein, 1975): trastuzumab, rituximab, adalimumab; also diagnostic kits (pregnancy tests) |
| Diagnostics | ELISA, PCR, DNA probes, biosensors |
| Gene therapy | Introducing a normal gene to correct a genetic defect |
| Antibiotics and enzymes | Industrial fermentation; streptokinase, asparaginase |
| Agriculture | Bt cotton and other transgenic crops |

**Benefits:** pure human proteins in large amounts, lower risk of allergy and infection than animal-derived products, new drugs for earlier untreatable diseases. **Concerns:** high cost, safety and ethical issues, need for cold storage (biologics are proteins).

## Remember

- Nucleotide = base + pentose + phosphate; nucleoside = base + pentose.
- Purines: adenine, guanine (two rings). Pyrimidines: cytosine, thymine (DNA), uracil (RNA).
- DNA: deoxyribose, double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953), antiparallel, right-handed, A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds), 10 base pairs and 3.4 nm per turn, 2 nm wide.
- RNA: ribose, uracil, single-stranded; mRNA carries codons, tRNA carries amino acids (cloverleaf, anticodon, CCA end), rRNA forms ribosomes.
- ATP = energy currency; cAMP = second messenger; NAD, FAD, CoA contain nucleotides.
- Biotechnology: restriction enzyme cuts, ligase joins, plasmid carries, E. coli/yeast makes – human insulin, hepatitis B vaccine, erythropoietin, interferons, monoclonal antibodies.

# Unit 5: Enzymes

This unit covers syllabus chapter 6 (5 hours).

## 5.1 Definition

**Enzymes** are **biological catalysts**: protein molecules (with very few exceptions) made by living cells that **speed up chemical reactions** in the body without being used up or permanently changed in the reaction.

- The substance on which an enzyme acts is the **substrate**; the substance formed is the **product**.
- The region of the enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction occurs is the **active site**.
- **Ribozymes** are RNA molecules that act as enzymes (for example the rRNA that forms peptide bonds) – the exception to "all enzymes are proteins".

### Parts of an enzyme

```text
   Holoenzyme (active)  =  Apoenzyme (protein part, inactive alone)
                           +  Cofactor (non-protein part)
                                 ├─ Metal ion activator (Zn2+, Mg2+, Fe2+, Cu2+)
                                 └─ Coenzyme (organic, often from a B vitamin)
                                       loosely bound   → coenzyme (NAD+, CoA)
                                       tightly bound   → prosthetic group (FAD, biotin)
```

| Coenzyme | Vitamin source | Carries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NAD+, NADP+ | Niacin | Hydrogen (hydride) |
| FAD, FMN | Riboflavin | Hydrogen |
| Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) | Thiamine | Aldehyde groups (decarboxylation) |
| Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) | Pyridoxine | Amino groups (transamination) |
| Coenzyme A | Pantothenic acid | Acyl groups |
| Biotin | Biotin | CO2 (carboxylation) |
| Tetrahydrofolate | Folic acid | One-carbon groups |

## 5.2 Properties of enzymes

1. **Catalytic power:** they raise reaction rates enormously (often a million times or more).
2. **Specificity:** each enzyme acts on one substrate or a group of related substrates.
   - **Absolute specificity:** one substrate only – urease acts only on urea.
   - **Group specificity:** a type of bond in many substrates – trypsin breaks peptide bonds next to lysine or arginine.
   - **Stereo-specificity:** only one optical isomer – L-amino acid oxidase acts only on L-amino acids.
   - **Reaction specificity:** one type of reaction only.
3. **Not consumed:** a small amount of enzyme handles a large amount of substrate.
4. **Do not change the equilibrium** of a reversible reaction; they only help it to be reached faster.
5. **Lower the activation energy** of the reaction.
6. **Sensitive to temperature and pH:** each has an optimum; being proteins they are denatured by heat and extremes of pH.
7. **Many need cofactors** (coenzymes or metal ions).
8. **Regulated:** activity is controlled by allosteric effectors, covalent modification (phosphorylation), induction and repression of synthesis.
9. **Some are made as inactive precursors** called **zymogens (proenzymes)** – pepsinogen, trypsinogen, prothrombin – which are activated when needed. This protects the tissue that makes them.
10. **Isoenzymes (isozymes):** different molecular forms of the same enzyme that catalyse the same reaction but differ in structure, tissue location and properties. Examples: **lactate dehydrogenase** (LDH1–LDH5; LDH1 rich in heart), **creatine kinase** (CK-MM in muscle, CK-MB in heart, CK-BB in brain). They help locate tissue damage.

## 5.3 IUB–MB classification of enzymes

The International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (IUBMB) classifies enzymes into classes according to the **type of reaction** they catalyse. Each enzyme gets a four-number **EC (Enzyme Commission) number**, such as EC 2.7.1.1 for hexokinase (class 2, transferase).

| Class | Name | Reaction | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **EC 1** | **Oxidoreductases** | Oxidation–reduction (transfer of H or electrons) | Lactate dehydrogenase, alcohol dehydrogenase, cytochrome oxidase, catalase |
| **EC 2** | **Transferases** | Transfer of a group (amino, phosphate, methyl) from one molecule to another | Hexokinase, transaminases (ALT, AST), creatine kinase |
| **EC 3** | **Hydrolases** | Breaking of bonds by adding water | Amylase, lipase, pepsin, trypsin, urease, acetylcholinesterase |
| **EC 4** | **Lyases** | Removal or addition of a group to a double bond without hydrolysis or oxidation | Aldolase, fumarase, carbonic anhydrase, decarboxylases |
| **EC 5** | **Isomerases** | Interconversion of isomers | Triose phosphate isomerase, phosphoglucomutase, epimerases |
| **EC 6** | **Ligases** (synthetases) | Joining two molecules using energy from ATP | Glutamine synthetase, DNA ligase, acetyl CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase |
| EC 7 | Translocases | Moving ions or molecules across membranes | Na+/K+-ATPase (class added in 2018; many textbooks still list six classes) |

Memory aid for the six classical classes: **"OTHLIL"** – Oxidoreductases, Transferases, Hydrolases, Lyases, Isomerases, Ligases.

## 5.4 Factors affecting enzyme activity

```text
 Rate                    Rate                     Rate
  │      ___ Vmax         │     /\                 │      /\
  │    /                  │    /  \                │     /  \
  │   /                   │   /    \               │    /    \
  │  /                    │  /      \              │   /      \
  │ /                     │ /        \             │  /        \
  └──────────── [S]       └──────────── Temp       └──────────── pH
   substrate conc.         optimum ~37 °C           optimum pH
   (hyperbola)             (denatured above)         (bell-shaped)
```

1. **Substrate concentration:** at low substrate concentration, rate rises almost in proportion; then the rise slows, and at high concentration the enzyme is **saturated** and the rate reaches a maximum (**Vmax**). The curve is a **rectangular hyperbola** (Michaelis–Menten kinetics).
   - **Km (Michaelis constant)** = the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax.
   - Low Km means **high affinity** of the enzyme for its substrate.
2. **Enzyme concentration:** with excess substrate, the rate is **directly proportional** to the enzyme concentration (a straight line). This is used to measure enzymes in serum.
3. **Temperature:** rate increases with temperature up to an **optimum** (about 37–40 °C for most human enzymes); above this the enzyme is denatured and activity falls sharply. Low temperature slows enzymes without destroying them (hence storage of enzymes and serum samples in the cold). Q10 (temperature coefficient): the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise in the working range.
4. **pH:** each enzyme has an **optimum pH**; activity falls on either side (bell-shaped curve) because ionisation of the active site and substrate changes. Pepsin works best at about pH 1.5–2, salivary amylase at about pH 6.8, trypsin at about pH 8, alkaline phosphatase at about pH 9–10.
5. **Product concentration:** accumulation of product slows the reaction (feedback or product inhibition).
6. **Activators:** metal ions (Mg2+ for kinases, Cl− for salivary amylase, Zn2+ for carbonic anhydrase).
7. **Inhibitors:** reduce activity (see 5.6).
8. **Time:** activity is constant over the early period and then falls as substrate is used up and the enzyme is slowly inactivated.
9. **Light and radiation:** UV and ionising radiation can inactivate enzymes.

## 5.5 Mechanism of action of enzymes

### Lowering the activation energy

Every reaction needs a minimum energy, the **activation energy**, for molecules to reach the reactive **transition state**. An enzyme provides an alternative pathway with a **lower activation energy**, so many more molecules react at body temperature.

```text
 Energy
   │        /‾‾\        ← without enzyme (high activation energy)
   │       /    \
   │      / /‾\  \      ← with enzyme (lower activation energy)
   │ S ──/ /   \  \
   │          ES  \
   │                \── P
   └───────────────────────── reaction progress
```

### Enzyme–substrate complex

The enzyme (E) binds the substrate (S) at its active site to form an **enzyme–substrate complex (ES)**, which changes to product (P) and releases the enzyme unchanged:

```text
   E + S  ⇌  ES  →  E + P
```

### Models of binding

**1. Lock and key model (Emil Fischer, 1894):** the active site has a rigid shape that exactly fits the substrate, as a key fits a lock. It explains specificity but not how some enzymes act on several related substrates.

**2. Induced fit model (Daniel Koshland, 1958):** the active site is flexible. When the substrate binds, the enzyme changes shape to fit it closely, like a glove fitting a hand. This brings catalytic groups into place and strains the substrate bonds. It is the accepted model today.

```text
 Lock and key:   [E with fixed pocket] + (S) → [E·S] → [E] + (P)
 Induced fit:    [E open pocket] + (S) → [E closes around S] → [E] + (P)
```

**How the enzyme speeds up the reaction:** bringing substrates close together in the right direction (proximity and orientation), straining bonds, acid–base catalysis by side chains, covalent catalysis and metal ion catalysis.

## 5.6 Enzyme inhibitors

An **inhibitor** is a substance that lowers the rate of an enzyme reaction.

```text
                 Enzyme inhibition
      ┌─────────────────┼────────────────────┐
  Reversible                         Irreversible
   ├ Competitive                      (covalent, permanent)
   ├ Non-competitive                 Suicide (mechanism-based)
   └ Uncompetitive                    Allosteric (regulatory)
```

### 1. Competitive inhibition

- The inhibitor **resembles the substrate** (structural analogue) and competes for the **same active site**.
- **Reversed by increasing substrate** concentration.
- **Km increases** (lower apparent affinity); **Vmax unchanged**.

| Inhibitor (drug) | Enzyme | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Malonate | Succinate dehydrogenase (TCA cycle) | Classic laboratory example |
| **Statins** (atorvastatin) | HMG-CoA reductase | Lower cholesterol |
| **Methotrexate** | Dihydrofolate reductase | Cancer, rheumatoid arthritis |
| **Sulphonamides** | Dihydropteroate synthase (bacterial; compete with PABA) | Antibacterial |
| **Allopurinol** | Xanthine oxidase | Gout (lowers uric acid) |
| Neostigmine | Acetylcholinesterase | Myasthenia gravis |
| Captopril | Angiotensin-converting enzyme | Hypertension |
| Ethanol | Alcohol dehydrogenase (competes with methanol) | Treatment of methanol poisoning |

### 2. Non-competitive inhibition

- The inhibitor binds at a site **other than the active site** (or to the ES complex), changing the enzyme so it works less well.
- **Not reversed** by adding more substrate.
- **Km unchanged**, **Vmax decreased**.
- Examples: heavy metals (Hg2+, Pb2+, Ag+) binding –SH groups; **cyanide** on cytochrome oxidase; fluoride on enolase (Mg2+ removal).

### 3. Uncompetitive inhibition

- The inhibitor binds only to the **enzyme–substrate complex**.
- **Both Km and Vmax decrease.** Example: lithium on inositol monophosphatase.

### 4. Irreversible inhibition

- The inhibitor forms a **covalent bond** with the enzyme and destroys its activity permanently; activity returns only when new enzyme is made.
- Examples: **organophosphate** insecticides and nerve gases on acetylcholinesterase; **aspirin** acetylates cyclooxygenase (so platelets cannot make thromboxane for their whole life); iodoacetate on glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase; disulfiram on aldehyde dehydrogenase.

### 5. Suicide (mechanism-based) inhibition

The enzyme converts an inactive substance into a reactive form that then destroys the enzyme. Example: **allopurinol** is changed by xanthine oxidase into **alloxanthine (oxypurinol)**, which binds tightly to the enzyme; **5-fluorouracil**; clavulanic acid on β-lactamase.

### 6. Allosteric (feedback) inhibition

A regulatory molecule binds at an **allosteric site** and changes enzyme activity. In **feedback inhibition**, the end product of a pathway inhibits the first enzyme: ATP and citrate inhibit phosphofructokinase; cholesterol inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.

### Comparison

| Feature | Competitive | Non-competitive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Binding site | Active site | Another site |
| Structure | Similar to substrate | Not similar |
| Effect of more substrate | Inhibition reversed | Not reversed |
| Km | Increased | Unchanged |
| Vmax | Unchanged | Decreased |
| Example | Malonate, statins | Heavy metals, cyanide |

## 5.7 Therapeutic and pharmaceutical importance of enzymes

### A. Enzymes used as drugs (therapeutic enzymes)

| Enzyme | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **Streptokinase**, **urokinase**, **alteplase (tPA)**, tenecteplase | Dissolve blood clots (thrombolytics) in heart attack, pulmonary embolism |
| **L-Asparaginase** | Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (removes asparagine needed by tumour cells) |
| **Pancreatin / pancrelipase** (amylase, lipase, protease) | Digestive aid in pancreatic insufficiency, cystic fibrosis |
| **Papain**, **bromelain** | Digestive aids, meat tenderiser, wound debridement |
| **Pepsin** | Digestive aid |
| **Serratiopeptidase**, **trypsin–chymotrypsin** | Reduce inflammation and swelling |
| **Hyaluronidase** | Increases spread and absorption of injected fluids and drugs |
| **Collagenase** | Removes dead tissue from burns and ulcers |
| **Dornase alfa (DNase)** | Thins the mucus in cystic fibrosis |
| **Lactase** | Lactose intolerance |
| Penicillinase | Treat penicillin allergic reactions (historical) |
| Enzyme replacement (imiglucerase) | Gaucher's disease |

### B. Diagnostic enzymes (clinical enzymology)

When cells are damaged, their enzymes leak into the blood. Raised serum levels help diagnosis:

| Enzyme | Raised in |
| --- | --- |
| **ALT (SGPT)** | Liver damage – hepatitis (more specific for liver) |
| **AST (SGOT)** | Liver disease, heart attack, muscle damage |
| **Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)** | Obstructive jaundice, bone disease (rickets, Paget's disease, bone cancer) |
| **Acid phosphatase** | Prostate cancer (now replaced largely by PSA) |
| **Amylase**, **lipase** | Acute pancreatitis |
| **CK-MB**, **LDH1** | Myocardial infarction (cardiac troponins are now preferred markers; they are proteins, not enzymes) |
| **γ-Glutamyl transferase (GGT)** | Alcoholic liver disease, obstructive jaundice |
| Cholinesterase (serum) | Lowered in organophosphate poisoning and liver disease |

### C. Enzymes as laboratory reagents (analytical enzymes)

Used in kits for estimating substances in blood and urine:

- **Glucose oxidase–peroxidase (GOD-POD)** – blood glucose, also urine dipsticks.
- **Urease** – blood urea.
- **Cholesterol oxidase and esterase** – serum cholesterol.
- **Uricase** – uric acid.
- **Horseradish peroxidase and alkaline phosphatase** – labels in ELISA.
- **Restriction enzymes, DNA ligase, Taq polymerase** – genetic engineering and PCR.

### D. Enzymes in pharmaceutical industry

Production of antibiotics (penicillin acylase to make semi-synthetic penicillins), steroid conversion, high-fructose syrup (glucose isomerase), cleaning agents and contact lens cleaners (proteases).

### E. Enzymes as drug targets

Most drugs act by inhibiting enzymes (see the inhibitor table): NSAIDs (cyclooxygenase), ACE inhibitors, statins, proton pump inhibitors (H+/K+-ATPase), MAO inhibitors, HIV protease inhibitors.

## Remember

- Enzymes are protein biological catalysts; they lower activation energy and do not change the equilibrium.
- Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor (coenzyme or metal ion); most coenzymes come from B vitamins.
- IUBMB classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases (OTHLIL); translocases added in 2018.
- Factors: substrate (hyperbola, Km = [S] at half Vmax), enzyme concentration, temperature (optimum ~37 °C), pH (bell curve), activators, inhibitors.
- Lock and key (Fischer) and induced fit (Koshland).
- Competitive: Km ↑, Vmax same (malonate, statins, methotrexate); non-competitive: Km same, Vmax ↓ (heavy metals, cyanide); irreversible: organophosphates, aspirin; suicide: allopurinol.
- Therapeutic: streptokinase, asparaginase, pancreatin, hyaluronidase; diagnostic: ALT, AST, ALP, amylase, CK-MB.
